correlates.name: Obstructive Shock: Pulmonary Embolism, Tension Pneumothorax, Cardiac Tamponade
correlates.presentation: all three share narrow pulse pressure, cool clammy extremities and poor capillary refill.
correlates.pathophysiology: PE and tension pneumothorax obstruct flow through the pulmonary circulation, so the RV strains against a high afterload and the LV is starved of preload.
correlates.treatment: fluid resuscitation plus relieving the obstruction - remove the embolus, decompress the pericardium or pleural space (Slide 34).

correlates.name: Septic Shock
correlates.presentation: SIRS = 2 of 4 - temperature > 38 or < 36 C, HR > 90, RR > 20 (or PaCO₂ < 32 mmHg), WBC > 12,000 or < 4,000 or > 10% immature bands. qSOFA = 2 of 3 - RR > 22, altered mentation, systolic BP < 100 (Slides 26-27).
correlates.pathophysiology: usually gram-negative bacteria acting through the endotoxin lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The lipid A portion binds the pattern-recognition receptor toll-like receptor 4 (TLR-4) on macrophages and B cells, stimulating IL-1, TNF and IL-6.
correlates.treatment: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within the first hour of diagnosis while awaiting blood cultures - vancomycin plus cefepime or piperacillin.

correlates.name: Anaphylactic Shock
correlates.presentation: throat and tongue swelling, coughing and wheezing, stridor, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, hives, urticaria, tachycardia, lethargy.
correlates.pathophysiology: an antigen-antibody reaction drives mast cells in the periphery and basophils in the blood to release histamine and histamine-like substances.
correlates.treatment: intramuscular epinephrine is the most important treatment; add normal saline for hypotension, oxygen, and albuterol for bronchospasm persisting after epinephrine (Slide 30).

correlates.name: Neurogenic Shock
correlates.presentation: like septic and anaphylactic shock - hypotension, wide pulse pressure, warm skin - except there is no tachycardia.
correlates.pathophysiology: dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system causing loss of sympathetic tone with an unopposed parasympathetic response, so the vasculature cannot constrict and the heart cannot mount a reflex response.

correlates.name: Vasopressor Complications
correlates.presentation: extravasation at the IV site with vasoconstriction of nearby connective tissue and skin necrosis; hypoperfusion of the extremities, mesenteric organs and kidneys with prolonged use.
correlates.pathophysiology: the same vasoconstriction that raises MAP shrinks the radius of vessels feeding tissue beds, so the drug that treats the shock simultaneously hypoperfuses organs.
correlates.treatment: treat the underlying cause so pressors can be weaned; monitor IV sites and distal perfusion.

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 agonism far outweighing beta-1 and beta-2, so systemic vascular resistance rises with a modest inotropic boost to cardiac output
drugs.indication: The usual first-choice vasopressor in distributive, cardiogenic and mixed shock
drugs.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias and digital ischemia; extravasation causes tissue necrosis

drugs.name: Phenylephrine
drugs.mechanism: Pure alpha-1 agonism raising systemic vascular resistance with no beta activity at all
drugs.indication: Distributive or hypovolemic shock in the patient whose tachyarrhythmia makes a beta agonist unattractive
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex bradycardia as the baroreflex answers the rise in afterload

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.mechanism: V1 and V2 receptor agonism raising vascular tone through a pathway entirely independent of adrenergic receptors
drugs.indication: The second agent added to norepinephrine in septic shock when a single pressor is not enough
drugs.adverseEffects: Arrhythmias and cardiac ischemia; splanchnic and digital hypoperfusion

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 greater than beta-1 greater than beta-2 agonism, raising heart rate, systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output together
drugs.indication: First line for anaphylaxis, given intramuscularly, and for cardiac arrest

drugs.name: Dopamine
drugs.mechanism: A dose-dependent mix of D1, beta-1, alpha-1 and beta-2 activity, which is why the lecturer calls it a messy drug
drugs.indication: Not first line for any shock state; occasionally used when bradycardia accompanies hypotension
drugs.adverseEffects: Arrhythmias and tissue ischemia progressing to gangrene

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.mechanism: Beta-1 dominant agonism that raises contractility and cardiac output — an inotrope, not a vasopressor
drugs.indication: Cardiogenic shock, where the primary insult is failing contractility rather than lost vascular tone
drugs.adverseEffects: Can cause hypotension, because beta-2 mediated vasodilation drops systemic vascular resistance

formulas.name: Systemic Vascular Resistance (Poiseuille)
formulas.meaning: Resistance depends on vessel radius to the fourth power, which is why arteriolar tone — not vessel length or blood viscosity — is what actually sets afterload
formulas.normalValue: Rises in hypovolemic, cardiogenic and obstructive shock; falls in distributive shock

formulas.name: Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation (SVO2)
formulas.equation: SVO2 = oxygen saturation of venous blood returning to the right heart
formulas.meaning: A read-out of how much oxygen the tissues extracted: high SVR slows capillary flow so extraction rises and SVO2 falls, while low SVR speeds flow so extraction falls and SVO2 rises
formulas.normalValue: Resuscitation target above 70%; a low SVR with a high SVO2 occurs in distributive shock and nowhere else

formulas.name: Shock Thresholds
formulas.equation: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg, or MAP < 65 mmHg
formulas.meaning: The pressure floor below which tissue perfusion is presumed inadequate and shock is declared, whatever the underlying mechanism
formulas.normalValue: Resuscitation targets are MAP above 65 mmHg and SVO2 above 70%

formulas.name: Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP)
formulas.equation: PCWP = left atrial pressure, measured by a Swan-Ganz catheter
formulas.meaning: The left-sided filling pressure, and the single measurement that splits obstructive shock into its pulmonary form (low PCWP) and its structural form (high PCWP)
formulas.normalValue: Low in hypovolemic and distributive shock, high in cardiogenic shock

formulas.name: Central Venous Pressure (CVP)
formulas.equation: CVP = right atrial pressure, the venous counterpart of PCWP
formulas.meaning: Reflects right atrial volume and pressure, so it falls whenever circulating volume or venous tone is lost and rises whenever the right heart cannot empty
formulas.normalValue: Low in hypovolemic and distributive shock, high in cardiogenic and obstructive shock
